headline: Yōbi is a back-formation of 月曜日 (getsuyōbi), 火曜日 (kayōbi) and the rest.
In sentan, 先 is a daiyōji replacing 尖.
Ōi ni is the continuative stem of the nari-adjective 大い (ōi).
Yowamaru is 弱 (yowa, root of 弱い, “weak”) plus -maru, “to become”.
Dokidoki is a reduplication of onomatopoeic doki, first attested in 1700; 動悸 (dōki, “heartbeat”) is apparently unrelated.
Amimono is ami, the stem of 編む (amu, “to knit”), plus 物 (-mono, “thing”).
Ikimono is 生き (iki, stem of 生きる, “to live”) plus 物 (-mono, “thing”).
Taiyō is from Middle Chinese 太陽, “sun”.
Tsugitsugi is a reduplication of 次 (tsugi, “next; following”).
Meue, “one's senior”, is 目 (me, “eye”) plus 上 (ue, “above”).
Yo no naka is 世 (yo) plus の (no) plus 中 (naka).
The spelling 寝間着 of nemaki is probably ateji (当て字).
Bunmei is a learned borrowing from Middle Chinese 文明.
Goku, “quite”, is from Middle Chinese 極 (MC gik).
Keru is from the Old Japanese verb 蹴う (kuu), from Proto-Japonic *kuw-a-.
Keiyōshi is 形容 (keiyō, “description; form”) plus 詞 (-shi, “word; part of speech”), first cited to 1870.
Masshiro is older 真白 (mashiro) with a doubled consonant for emphasis, first cited to around 1500.
Mazeru is from Old Japanese mazu, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720, cognate with Okinawan 混じゆん (majiyun).
Onna no hito is 女 (onna, “female person, woman”) plus の (no) plus 人 (hito, “person”).
Daihyō is a learned borrowing from Chinese 代表 (dàibiǎo).
Fuka is the prefix 不 (fu-) plus 可 (ka).
Toku, “to explain”, is cognate with 解く (toku).
Chotto is from ちっと (chitto), a geminated emphatic form of ちと (chito), first attested in 1477.
Teiryūjo is 停留 (teiryū) plus 所 (-sho), in its rendaku form 所 (jo).
Naru, “to bear fruit”, is cognate with 成る (naru, “become”).
Kayō is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 歌謠 (gēyáo).
Teika is tei (定, fixed) plus ka (価, monetary value).
Shujutsu is 手 (shu, “hand”) plus 術 (-jutsu, “technique”), presumably a Meiji calque of Ancient Greek kheirourgía.
Resutoran is from French restaurant, possibly via English restaurant.
Chairoi is 茶色 (chairo) plus い (-i).
Kage, “shade”, is from Proto-Japonic *kankay, cognate with 影 (kage, “shadow”).
